title: The filesystem hierarchy, paths and file operations
summary: Where things live on a Fedora system, how paths resolve, and the operations you type daily — with the details that matter during an incident.

sections.heading: FHS: where things live
sections.html:
PathContentsInterview note
/etcHost-specific configurationPackage defaults live in /usr/share/ or /usr/lib/; never edit those
/varVariable data: logs, spools, databases, caches/var/log growing without limit is a classic outage
/usrRead-only user data: binaries, libraries, share/usr/bin vs /usr/local/bin vs /bin (symlink to /usr/bin on Fedora)
/homeUser dataOften a separate mount, which is why quotas and disk-full behave per-filesystem
/tmpTemporary, world-writable, often tmpfsCleared on reboot; never store anything you need
/runRuntime state, tmpfs, recreated each bootPID files and sockets used to live in /var/run (now a symlink)
/proc, /sysKernel interfaces presented as filesTuning knobs: /proc/sys/net/...
/optAdd-on software packagesThird-party agents

sections.heading: Absolute versus relative, and the ones people forget
sections.html:
An absolute path starts at /; a relative path resolves from the current working directory. The special entries matter more than they look:

  • . — current directory, .. — parent.
  • ~ — your home; ~user — another user's home.
  • - — previous directory (cd -).
  • A leading / on a path inside a config file is a frequent bug: log=/var/log/app.log vs log=var/log/app.log resolves relative to the service's working directory, which for systemd is / but for a manual run is wherever you typed the command.

sections.heading: The operations, with the gotchas
sections.html:
CommandUseGotcha
cpCopy-a preserves mode, owner, timestamps; plain cp does not, which silently changes ownership on config restores
mvMove/renameAcross filesystems it is copy+delete, so inode and ACLs change
rmDeleteNo trash, no undo; rm -rf on a mistyped variable is an outage. Use -- before paths starting with -
ln -sSymlinkRelative targets break when the link moves; ln -sf silently replaces, including replacing a directory link
findSearch by metadataTraverses, so -xdev and pruning matter on big trees
grep -rSearch contentFollows symlinks only with -R; binary files need -a
locateSearch a databaseDatabase is periodically rebuilt; results are stale by default
tarArchive-C changes directory before archiving — the safest way to avoid absolute paths in archives

The two commands worth memorising as patterns:

# files larger than 100MB, across the whole filesystem, one filesystem onlyfind / -xdev -type f -size +100M -printf '%s\t%p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head
# files modified in the last 2 hours (change analysis after an incident)find /etc -mmin -120 -type f
# which config file actually contains this setting?grep -rn --include='*.conf' 'MaxClients' /etc

That last one is the practical way to answer 'where is this setting coming from' — far better than guessing between /etc/app/app.conf and a distro default in /usr/lib/.

sections.heading: Hard links versus symbolic links
sections.html:
A hard link is another name for the same inode: same data, same permissions, and it survives deleting the original. A symlink is a small file containing a path, resolved at access time.

$ ls -li262145 -rw-r--r--. 2 root root   42 Nov 17 10:00 app.conf
262146 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root   14 Nov 17 10:00 current -> releases/v2/
262145 -rw-r--r--. 2 root root   42 Nov 17 10:00 app.conf.bak   # same inode, link count 2

Hard links cannot cross filesystems and cannot point at directories. Symlinks can, but break when the target moves — the classic cause of a service failing to start after a 'harmless' directory rename.

checks.prompt: Which command finds files over 500MB on the root filesystem without descending into other mounts?
checks.explanation: -xdev stays on one filesystem; -type f restricts to files; -size +500M filters by size.

why_wrong.3: It descends into every mount, including slow network filesystems.
why_wrong.2: locate searches names, not sizes, and is indexed.
why_wrong.0: du summarises directories, it does not find files.

checks.prompt: A service starts fine manually but fails when started by systemd, complaining about a relative path. Why?
options: systemd runs with a different working directory
checks.explanation: A manually started service inherits your shell's cwd; systemd's default WorkingDirectory is /. Relative paths therefore resolve differently.

why_wrong.2: Relative paths are legal, they just resolve against a different base.
why_wrong.3: The file exists — it worked manually.
why_wrong.0: SELinux does not distinguish relative and absolute paths.

connect.text: Every path component needs traversal permission, which is why a readable file can still be unreadable.

interview.q: Where would you look for the configuration of an installed service?
interview.a: Start with /etc (and /etc/<name>/); check the unit file for EnvironmentFile and command-line options; the package defaults usually live under /usr/lib or /usr/share, which you should not edit. grep -r over /etc finds the effective file quickly.

interview.q: What is the difference between a hard link and a symlink?
interview.a: A hard link is a second directory entry for the same inode — same data, no separate file, cannot cross filesystems or reference directories. A symlink is a separate file holding a path that is resolved at access time, so it can cross filesystems but breaks if the target moves.
